svg.title: The memory-capacity paradigm on a human connectome
svg.desc: A random scalar input drives a human connectome used as the fixed recurrent layer of an echo-state network. A ridge readout reconstructs the input tau steps in the past; the squared correlation on held-out data, r2(tau), is the forgetting curve and its sum over delays is the memory capacity (MC = 8.08 for this connectome, stable rank 3.34). With the weights around each region made uniform on the same wiring, the stable rank is 2.52 and MC = 7.61.

g.text: A scalar random input u(t) is injected into the 90 regions of one human connectome through fixed random weights Win.
The connectome is the reservoir: its weights W are rescaled to spectral radius ρ(W) = 0.99 and never trained.
A linear readout, trained by ridge regression, reconstructs the input τ steps in the past from the present state r(t).
Its accuracy on held-out data is the squared correlation r2(τ) between the delayed input and its reconstruction.

text.tspan: (τ) decays with the delay: the forgetting curve. Its sum is the memory capacity, MC = Σ

g.text: MC measures how much of the past input stays linearly decodable from the present state of the connectome.
Same wiring, but the weights around every region are made uniform. The stable rank rs of the network falls, and memory with it.
The arrangement of the connection weights, not the wiring diagram alone, sets how much past input the network retains.
r(t+1) = tanh[ Win u(t+1) + W r(t) ]
90 regions · HCP Young Adult participant, 27 y
